sampling_model.design: A triangular array of binary sequential experiments with fixed finite-population potential outcomes and assignment as the only randomness.
sampling_model.treatment: Given \(\mathcal F_{n,t-1}\), \(A_{nt}\) is Bernoulli with known logged predictable probability \(e_{nt}\).
sampling_model.overlap: The rare-arm probability follows \(t e_{nt}\approx \bar q(t/n)\) after an early cutoff, with bounded cumulative hazard and \(0<e_{nt}\le\rho<1\).
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: Predictable regressions \(m_{nt}(a)\) may be arbitrary within their bound; their treated residuals follow a deterministic Lipschitz profile on one common high-probability event.
sampling_model.randomness: Only the known adaptive randomization law is random; there is no superpopulation sampling assumption.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: If Condition 3 holds, the standardized AIPW estimator converges in distribution to a standard normal law.
Theorem 1 constructs doubly robust betting confidence sequences under predictable logging.
Proposition 1 proves selective type-I error control for the selective randomization p-value.
Theorem 1 proves asymptotic type-I error control for simulation with optimism in specified adaptive designs.
Proposition 2 gives an exact compound-Poisson law for an HT rate estimator under independent Poisson importance sampling.
Finite-population limited-overlap estimators are asymptotically Gaussian when their effective sample size diverges.
Any valid i.i.d. bounded-mean confidence interval obeys an inverse-information-projection width lower bound.
Stein perturbation yields explicit total-variation compound-Poisson approximation bounds for integer-valued sums.
Weighted Bernoulli and Poisson sums admit generalized Dickman approximation bounds.
Theorem 1 gives a semiparametrically efficient Gaussian limit for the truncated A2IPW estimator.
Resampling simulations find tighter superior-arm and wider inferior-arm intervals under real-time adaptive randomization.

body.tldr: At the critical rare-arm boundary, where the cumulative allocation hazard is bounded, the finite-population AIPW error is not generically Gaussian. The project constructs a stopped coupling from the adaptive assignment process to an independent Bernoulli array and then to a signed marked Poisson integral, with an explicit finite-experiment error budget. A directed-rational profile-net convolution calibrates an atom-safe confidence interval from the completed propensity log using an explicit dyadic bandwidth bracket whose radius charge is at most \(5\cdot2^{-n}\). The main theorem gives uniform randomization coverage and an oracle radius inequality with explicit level and radius slack. A separate complete-experiment void-event argument shows that every \(95\%\)-honest confidence set has diameter at least \(1/8\) with limiting probability at least \(0.60710678\) on an exact late-ramp pair, while a legal high-hazard subfamily has robust limiting radius at most \(0.442M\) apart from the declared slack and dyadic charge.

project_justification.gap: Li and Zhao establish design-based Gaussian AIPW inference under variance-convergence and Lindeberg conditions, and Waudby-Smith et al. establish generic anytime-valid martingale intervals under predictable logging. Neither result calibrates the discontinuous signed compound-Poisson law that remains when rare-arm cumulative hazard is bounded, nor does either derive an all-confidence-set width obstruction from the complete logged experiment.
project_justification.niche: The bounded-hazard boundary is statistically distinct: only finitely many informative rare assignments survive in the limit, atoms cannot be handled by routine quantile convergence, and a threshold selected from the completed propensity log must be protected against same-log selection.
project_justification.fill: The project supplies a computable adaptive-to-Bernoulli-to-Poisson transfer, a simultaneous profile enclosure and directed convolution certificate, an explicit directed-dyadic bandwidth with a vanishing radius charge, an atom-safe coverage and oracle-radius theorem, and a separate void-event lower bound for arbitrary confidence sets.

body.related_work: Li and Zhao (2026) provide the closest setup and writing model: fixed potential outcomes, adaptive assignment as the only randomness, and an AIPW martingale decomposition. Their Condition 3 and Theorem 4 deliver Gaussian inference only after variance convergence and Lindeberg, whereas the present critical profiles retain order-one rare-arm increments. Bibaut and Kallus (2024) organize adaptive inference into martingale-CLT repair, always-valid methods, and direct inversion of nonnormal laws; their review identifies the last route as incomplete beyond special settings. Waudby-Smith et al. (2024) provide exact predictable-logging martingale confidence sequences without a global importance-weight bound; their generic boundaries inform the safety architecture but do not determine the signed atomic profile radius. Freidling, Zhao, and Gao (2026) condition exact randomization tests on adaptive selection; the present calibration instead uses deterministic threshold domination because conditioning on the completed propensity log cannot create an independent Bernoulli reference. Cho, Bibaut, and Kallus (2025) invert simulated nonnormal adaptive laws under stochastic bandit models; the proposed interval is design-based and uses certified outward error rather than Monte Carlo approximation. Chen et al. (2026) derive an exact compound-Poisson HT rate model under independent Poisson importance sampling and propose monotone bootstrap intervals; their result neither treats a signed causal contrast under adaptive assignment nor supplies uniform finite-experiment coverage. Hong, Leung, and Li (2020) treat finite-population limited overlap in a diverging-effective-information regime. Shekhar and Ramdas (2023) derive i.i.d. bounded-mean width lower bounds; the proposed lower bound acts on the complete sequential experiment through its shared void atom. Barbour and Xia (1999) motivate explicit coupling and Stein error accounting for compound-Poisson approximation, while Bhattacharjee and Goldstein (2019) identify the constant-profile Dickman reduction. Liberali et al. (2025) are the applied consumer: their delayed-endpoint GUSTO-1 and EUROPA simulations document inferior-arm interval inflation but do not prove conditional finite-population coverage.
body.technical_internal_limitation: The finite-transfer theorem couples the AIPW statistic, not the complete statistical experiments. It cannot by itself imply an information bound for arbitrary estimators; Theorem \(\mathrm{7}\) therefore uses a separate shared-subprobability argument. The deterministic profiles are fixed before the path is realized. A claim that a suitable profile exists only after observing outcomes would invalidate the threshold comparison. Exact no-slack quantile convergence is not asserted at atoms. The high-hazard result is an upper bound on a declared subfamily, not a globally sharp minimax-width constant.
body.honest_scope: The open core is the independently checked end-to-end proof and implementation of the stopped coupling, rational profile enclosure, signed convolution, and deterministic threshold allocation over the full declared class. The directed-dyadic bandwidth is explicit and vanishes, with a reported-radius charge bounded by \(5\cdot2^{-n}\). The separate computational question asks for polynomial bit complexity in \(n\), total rational input length \(\Lambda_n\), and \(\xi^{-1}\) under the stated certified pruning invariant. The \(16\)-bin ramp computation and high-hazard Chebyshev arithmetic are reproducible diagnostics, not substitutes for the uniform theorem. The application to Liberali et al. is conditional on a prespecified expected-endpoint bridge that verifies the deterministic profile and modulus contract. Random profile or Cox-process extensions, exact atom-free quantile claims, and globally optimal expected-width constants are outside scope. Under the homogeneous-residual constant-intensity special case, the law reduces to the known generalized Dickman result in Proposition \(\mathrm{11}\).
